passage: In the adolescent clinic waiting room, Tushar kept folding and unfolding the appointment slip. Beside him, his daughter Ira stared at a poster about handwashing. Last night, reaching past her for the salt, he had seen the fresh marks on her forearm before she tugged her sleeve down. Fear had hit first, then a hot wave of anger: How could you? Why didn't you tell me? Then guilt: How did I miss this? He had wanted to shout. Instead he had put the salt down, sat on the kitchen floor beside her and said, "I'm not angry with you. I'm frightened, and I love you. We'll get help together." This morning he had called the family doctor, who fitted them in here. Now Ira leaned, just slightly, against his shoulder. "Ira?" the nurse called. Tushar stood. "Want me to come in, or wait here?" "Come in," she said.

qa.q: Where are Tushar and Ira waiting?
qa.a: In the adolescent clinic waiting room.

qa.q: What feelings did Tushar go through after seeing the marks?
qa.a: Fear first, then a hot wave of anger, then guilt about how he had missed it.

qa.q: Which choice in the kitchen protected the bond between Tushar and Ira?
qa.a: Instead of shouting, he sat beside her, said he was frightened and loved her, and promised they'd get help together, then called the doctor next morning.

qa.q: How might Ira have experienced Tushar's calm response?
qa.a: She may have felt safe rather than punished, which is why she leaned on him and asked him to come in.

grounding: It shows a parent who discovers signs of self-harm feeling fear, anger and guilt, and choosing calm concern and professional help over punishment or panic.

passage:
Vikas beta,
I'm writing because when I try to say this aloud, my voice shakes.
Yesterday, when I found the bandages in your drawer and you told me why, I panicked. I shouted, I took your phone, I said things like "How could you do this to us?" That was my fear talking, and it was wrong. You were hurting, and I made it about me. I'm sorry.
Here is what I know now. I'm not angry with you. I'm scared, and I feel guilty that I didn't see how bad things were. None of that is yours to fix.
Last night, once calmer, I rang a parents' helpline. This morning I phoned the school counsellor. She gave us the name of a psychologist who works with teenagers, and we have an appointment on Thursday. I can come in with you, or wait outside, whichever you choose.
Your phone is back on your desk.
Love always,
Mummy (Alka)

qa.q: When is the appointment with the psychologist?
qa.a: On Thursday.

qa.q: What does Alka feel now, looking back on yesterday?
qa.a: Alka feels scared, guilty for not seeing how bad things were, and sorry for shouting.

qa.q: What turned Alka's panic into a helpful response?
qa.a: Alka rang a helpline that night, apologised, said she wasn't angry, returned the phone and arranged a psychologist through the school counsellor, letting Vikas choose how involved she would be.

qa.q: How might Vikas feel finding the phone back on the desk with the letter?
qa.a: Vikas may read it as a sign of trust, and feel that help is being offered, not punishment.

grounding: It shows a mother who reacted to signs of self-harm with panic, then turns to calm concern, an apology and a psychologist to protect the bond and safety.

passage:
Nilesh,
Last night, when I saw the marks on your arm, I felt so many things at once. Fear first. Then guilt, wondering how I didn't see. And, I'm ashamed to say, anger, and I raised my voice. I'm sorry for that.
Then I sat down next to you and said, "I'm not angry with you. I'm frightened because I love you." I stayed up with you, and we called the helpline together before we slept. You let me hold your hand.
I won't punish you. I won't take away your phone or your friends. I have booked an appointment with a psychologist for Thursday, and I'll come with you, or wait outside, whichever you want.
Nothing you've done makes me love you less.
Your Amma, Damini

qa.q: When is the appointment with the psychologist?
qa.a: On Thursday.

qa.q: How did Damini feel on seeing the marks?
qa.a: Damini felt fear first, then guilt at not seeing it, and anger, which led to a raised voice.

qa.q: What did Damini do that protected both Nilesh's safety and their bond?
qa.a: Damini apologised for shouting, stayed calm and close, called the helpline with Nilesh that night, ruled out punishment and arranged a psychologist.

qa.q: How might Nilesh feel reading "Nothing you've done makes me love you less"?
qa.a: Nilesh may feel relieved and safe, knowing Amma is not angry and will stand by Nilesh.

grounding: Shows a parent who discovers signs of self-harm, feels fear, guilt and anger, and responds with calm concern and professional help rather than punishment.

passage: I'm Minakshi, Bidisha's mother. I found out in March, when I saw a bandage she hadn't mentioned and then the marks under it. My first reaction was panic. I wanted to scream, to ask what I had done wrong, to lock away everything in the house. I was so angry, but mostly at myself. I went into the bathroom and breathed for two minutes. Then I sat on her bed and said, "I'm not angry with you. I'm here, and we'll get help together." She cried and cried. I didn't leave her that night. We called the helpline, and the next morning I took her to our doctor, who referred us to a psychologist. If I'd punished her, I think I'd have lost her trust. Instead, she talks to me now.

qa.q: What did Minakshi first notice?
qa.a: A bandage Bidisha hadn't mentioned, and then the marks under it.

qa.q: How did Minakshi feel when she found out?
qa.a: She felt panic, anger mostly at herself, and a wish to scream, before calming herself.

qa.q: What did Minakshi do that protected Bidisha's safety and trust?
qa.a: She calmed herself, told Bidisha she wasn't angry, stayed with her that night, called the helpline and took her to the doctor the next morning.

qa.q: How might Bidisha have felt when her mother said "We'll get help together"?
qa.a: Bidisha likely felt relief and safety, which is why she cried and now talks to her mother.

grounding: Shows a parent who discovers self-harm signs, feels fear, guilt and anger, and responds with calm concern and professional help rather than punishment or panic.

passage:
Monday: Sudha noticed her son Ojas, fifteen, wearing full sleeves in the May heat and locking his door for hours.
Thursday: Passing the bathroom, she saw a fresh bandage on his wrist. Her heart pounded; she wanted to shout, "What have you done?" Instead she knocked and sat beside him on his bed. "I'm not angry. I'm worried, and I love you. Will you tell me what's happening?" Ojas cried and said he'd been hurting himself when things got too much. Sudha held him. She didn't leave him alone that night. They called the helpline together, and she slept on the mattress on his floor.
Saturday: They sat together in a psychologist's office. On the way home, Ojas said, "Thanks for not yelling, Amma."

qa.q: What did Sudha see on Ojas's wrist on Thursday?
qa.a: A fresh bandage.

qa.q: How did Sudha feel when she saw the bandage?
qa.a: She felt frightened, her heart pounding, and wanted to shout, but chose calm concern.

qa.q: What did Sudha do on Thursday night that kept Ojas safe?
qa.a: She stayed calm, listened, didn't leave him alone, called the helpline with him and slept on his floor.

qa.q: How might Ojas feel about his mother after Saturday?
qa.a: Ojas may feel grateful and closer to her, thanking her for not yelling.

grounding: Shows a parent who discovers self-harm signs and responds with calm concern rather than punishment, staying with her son and arranging professional help.

passage:
Madhuri, you start teaching Class 9 next month. Vivek said I could tell you this, so listen to your Harsha Mama.
When my son Vivek was fifteen, I found marks on his arm one evening when his sleeve slipped. My first feeling was pure fear. Then guilt: how had I not seen? Then, God forgive me, anger. I wanted to shout, "What have you done?"
I didn't. I sat on the floor of his room and took three breaths. I said, "I'm not angry with you. I'm scared, and I love you. Can you tell me what's been hurting?"
He cried. I held him. That same night, your Mami and I called a helpline with him, and the next morning we saw a psychologist.
It took a long time. But he still talks to me, Madhuri. If I'd shouted, I don't think he would.

qa.q: How old was Vivek when Harsha Mama found the marks?
qa.a: Fifteen.

qa.q: How did Harsha Mama feel when he first found the marks?
qa.a: He felt fear, then guilt for not seeing it, then anger, all within moments.

qa.q: What turning point in the story protected both the bond and Vivek's safety?
qa.a: Harsha Mama chose calm concern over shouting, told Vivek he loved him, and got help the same night through a helpline, then a psychologist.

qa.q: What might Vivek have felt when his father sat on the floor instead of shouting?
qa.a: He probably felt relief and safety, enough to cry and start talking.

grounding: Harsha Mama tells how, finding signs of self-harm in his son, he felt fear, guilt and anger but responded with calm concern and arranged professional help.
